title: My Eyes Have Seen You: Job Restored
summary: Job answers God for the last time: God can do all things, Job spoke of what he didn't understand, and now, having seen God, he retracts his words and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD then rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking of him accurately, as Job has, and tells them to offer sacrifices while Job prays for them. After Job prays, God restores his fortunes double, gives him seven sons and three daughters, and Job lives to see four generations.
story: The book ends where it began, in prose. The opening chapters told of a heavenly test and Job's loss of everything; the long poem that followed gave voice to his anguish, the friends' arguments, Elihu's speeches, and finally God's answer from the whirlwind. Now Job responds to that answer, and the narrator closes the story. God's verdict on the debate comes in verses 7 and 8, and it is surprising: the friends, who defended God, are rebuked, and Job, who protested, is called God's servant who spoke accurately. Job becomes the priest who intercedes for those who wronged him. Then the losses of chapter 1 are reversed, though the book never tells Job about the test in heaven. It ends with a man old and full of years.
historical:
The epilogue keeps the patriarchal atmosphere of the prologue. Job acts as priest for others, as heads of families did before Israel had a priesthood (compare Genesis 8:20, 22:13). Wealth is counted in flocks and herds, and his lifespan of 140 more years recalls the long lives of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The piece of silver each visitor brings (verse 11) is a qesitah, an old unit of value otherwise found only in the stories of Jacob (Genesis 33:19) and in Joshua 24:32, which also points to an early setting or a deliberately archaic one. The Greek translation of Job (part of the Septuagint) adds a postscript identifying Job with Jobab, a king of Edom listed in Genesis 36:33, a tradition that reflects later speculation rather than the Hebrew text.

The restoration doubles Job's livestock exactly: the numbers in verse 12 are twice those in 1:3. His children are restored in the same number, seven sons and three daughters. Ezekiel's reference to Job among the righteous men of old (Ezekiel 14:14, 20) and James's reference to Job's perseverance (James 5:11) show that later readers knew his story as a whole, including this ending.
cultural:
Several customs in the chapter reward attention. The sacrifice of seven bulls and seven rams was a large and costly offering, reflecting the seriousness of the friends' fault; seven was the number of completeness. Comforters bringing gifts (verse 11) was a way of restoring a person's standing in the community after disaster, since the family and friends who had stayed away during his affliction (19:13-19) now come to eat with him, an act of full reconciliation.

The naming of Job's daughters is unusual. Biblical genealogies and stories usually name sons and leave daughters unnamed, but here the three daughters are named and the sons are not. Their names suggest beauty and luxury: Jemimah probably means dove, Keziah is the name of the fragrant spice cassia, and Keren-happuch means horn of eye-paint, a container for the dark cosmetic used around the eyes. Job also gives them an inheritance alongside their brothers, which went beyond Israel's later law, where daughters inherited only if there were no sons (Numbers 27:1-11).
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 6 are poetry, Job's final reply, in which he quotes God's own words from 38:2-3 and 40:7 and responds to them. The hinge of the whole book is verse 5: “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” Verses 7 to 17 return to prose and form the epilogue, which mirrors the prologue in reverse. The friends who came to comfort Job in 2:11 are now rebuked; the relatives who abandoned him come to comfort him; the servant language of 1:8 (my servant Job) returns four times in verses 7 and 8; and the wealth and children lost in chapter 1 are restored. The closing phrase, old and full of years, is the same used for Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 25:8, 35:29).

outline.t: Job's final reply: I have seen you
God rebukes the friends and accepts Job's prayer
Job's fortunes restored and his family returns
Double blessing, seven sons, and three daughters
Job dies old and full of years

doctrines.note: Job's repentance is not a confession of the sins the friends charged him with, since God immediately affirms him. It is a turning from his presumption to speak of what he did not understand, in the light of seeing God. Repentance here is a change of stance before God, not a plea bargain.

God tells the friends that Job will pray for them and that he will accept Job's prayer. The sufferer becomes the intercessor for those who hurt him, and God's restoration of Job comes after he prays for his friends.

Job confesses that God can do all things and that no plan of his can be thwarted. The book ends not with an explanation of suffering but with trust in the God whose purposes stand, even when they are hidden.

The restoration does not explain Job's suffering or erase it, and Job is never told about the test in heaven. The book affirms that God is not indifferent to the sufferer and that the last word belongs to his compassion.

words.note: Nacham, translated repent in verse 6. The verb's range includes to be sorry, to change one's mind, and to be comforted or consoled. Some scholars translate the verse as Job being comforted concerning dust and ashes, that is, finding consolation in his mortal condition. The BSB's reading, repenting in dust and ashes, is the traditional one. Either way, Job's stance toward God has changed.

Maas, to reject or despise. In verse 6 it has no stated object in Hebrew, so translations supply one: I retract my words (BSB), I despise myself, or I reject what I said. The ambiguity is part of the verse's difficulty, and it warns against building too much on any single translation.

Kun, here in a form meaning what is right, correct, or firmly true. God says twice that the friends have not spoken of him accurately, as Job has. The word suggests speech that corresponds to reality. Job's raw protests turn out to have been more truthful about God than the friends' neat theology.

Shevut, often in the phrase to restore the fortunes, and traditionally translated captivity. In verse 10 the LORD restores Job's fortunes, the same phrase later used of God restoring Israel after exile. Job's story becomes a pattern of the restoration God promises to his people.

christ: Job's story ends with a righteous sufferer vindicated by God, interceding for those who wronged him, and restored beyond his former state. The New Testament does not call Job a prophecy of Christ, but the pattern is hard to miss. Jesus, the truly innocent sufferer, prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), was vindicated by God in his resurrection, and now intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25). James holds Job up as an example: “You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.” (James 5:11). The outcome James has in mind is the ending of this chapter, and for Christian readers it anticipates a greater outcome, the resurrection, in which what was lost is not replaced but restored.

hard.q: Does the happy ending undo the book's message, and can new children replace the ones Job lost?
hard.a:
Many readers feel uneasy with the epilogue. The book has argued at length that righteousness and prosperity don't always go together, and then it ends by giving Job double prosperity. Some critics think the ending was part of an older folk tale that the poet kept without fully endorsing. Others argue that it doesn't undo the message, because Job receives his restoration only after he has let go of his demand for it, and because it comes as a free gift, not a reward he could claim. The book as a whole says that God is free, not bound by a formula, and that includes his freedom to bless.

The loss of Job's first children is not erased, and the text doesn't pretend otherwise; no new child replaces a lost one. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters have noted that Job's livestock doubled while his children were restored only in the same number, and have suggested that his first children were not lost forever but still counted as his, awaiting a future beyond death. That reading is an inference the text doesn't state, and interpreters differ on it. What the text does say is that Job lived to see four generations and died old and full of years, with grief behind him and blessing around him.

questions: Job says, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” What is the difference between knowing about God and meeting him?
God rebukes the friends for speaking wrongly about him, even though they were defending him. How might our efforts to defend God sometimes misrepresent him?
Job prays for the friends who hurt him before his fortunes are restored. What would it look like for you to pray for someone who has wounded you?
